column3: A large cylindrical prolapse on straining in an 84-year-old is full-thickness rectal prolapse; start with stool softeners and bowel-habit advice, then Delorme or rectopexy if needed.
A fluctuant natal-cleft swelling with midline pits is a pilonidal abscess: incision and drainage (off the midline); definitive excision later once the sepsis settles.
An acute perianal abscess over a known fistula needs examination under anaesthesia with incision and drainage (and laying open or seton of any fistula found).
A posterior midline fissure is treated first with topical diltiazem (or GTN) plus stool softeners; botulinum toxin or lateral sphincterotomy if it fails.
Melaena, epigastric pain, weight loss and a Virchow node suggest gastric cancer: OGD with biopsy is needed for tissue diagnosis, then CT for staging.
Coffee-ground vomiting is upper GI bleeding: OGD (within 24 h, sooner if unstable) to find and treat the source.
Haematemesis with jaundice and ascites in an alcoholic suggests portal hypertension and bleeding oesophageal varices.

A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after fainting at home. He has passed bright red blood per rectum for 6 hours, without abdominal pain or vomiting. Pulse 110/min, BP 95/50 mmHg; there is gross blood on rectal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Sudden painless massive bright-red rectal bleeding in an older patient is most often diverticular.

A 56-year-old woman had an episode of melaena 48 hours ago that has not recurred. She had an abdominal aortic aneurysm repair 2 years ago. Upper GI endoscopy to the duodenal bulb and colonoscopy are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A ‘herald’ GI bleed after aortic graft surgery is an aortoenteric fistula (usually 3rd/4th part of duodenum) until proven otherwise: CT angiography.

A 65-year-old woman has severe fatigue and weakness. She has hypertension, diabetes and coronary disease, takes daily aspirin and has a 40 pack-year smoking history. She is pale, her stool is positive for occult blood and she has a microcytic anaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
G
Occult bleeding with iron-deficiency anaemia in an older patient is colorectal (often right-sided) cancer until proven otherwise: colonoscopy.

A 65-year-old man has haematemesis and melaena. He has had abdominal pain for 3–4 weeks and has taken ibuprofen four times daily for 3 weeks, with alcohol, for the pain. Pulse 100/min, BP 100/60 mmHg after resuscitation; there is RUQ and epigastric tenderness and melaena on rectal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
I
Regular NSAIDs and alcohol cause gastric mucosal ulceration; a bleeding gastric ulcer is most likely.

A 50-year-old man with chronic alcoholism has an episode of haematemesis. Pulse 120/min, BP 90/60 mmHg; there are spider naevi, palmar erythema and a distended, non-tender abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
H
Stigmata of chronic liver disease with haematemesis and shock point to bleeding oesophageal varices.

A 35-year-old man has haematemesis and black tarry stools after 2 weeks of epigastric pain partly relieved by antacids. Pulse 110/min, BP 95/60 mmHg, with epigastric tenderness and melaena. What is the most likely diagnosis?
F
Epigastric pain relieved by antacids followed by haematemesis and melaena is a bleeding peptic (usually duodenal) ulcer.

A 35-year-old woman has a 1-week history of bloody diarrhoea, 1 month of abdominal pain and 10 lb weight loss. Temperature 38.3 °C, pulse 85/min, BP 110/60 mmHg; the abdomen is diffusely tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Bloody diarrhoea with fever and weight loss in a young adult suggests ulcerative colitis.

New constipation with narrow stools and dark-red bleeding in an elderly woman is left-sided colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.
Massive lower GI bleeding with shock and no source on examination: after resuscitation (and OGD if upper source possible), CT/mesenteric angiography localises and allows embolisation.
Years of bright-red blood on the paper without bowel change suggests haemorrhoids: proctoscopy/rigid sigmoidoscopy in clinic first; colonoscopy if red flags.
Profuse rectal bleeding with shock: resuscitation comes first — two large-bore cannulae, bloods, cross-match and fluids/blood — before investigations.
Variceal bleeding continuing after banding needs immediate senior help for rescue therapy (balloon tamponade, repeat endoscopy or TIPS); bloods and imaging do not stop the bleeding.
A duodenal ulcer is usually associated with H. pylori, shown by a positive rapid urease (CLO) test on gastric biopsy.
Microcytic anaemia in a 79-year-old suggests occult GI blood loss: OGD (with colonoscopy/CT) to find the source, starting here with OGD given the epigastric pain.
Free gas under the diaphragm with epigastric pain in a patient on NSAIDs and steroids is a perforated peptic ulcer; steroids can mask peritonism.
Melaena with a raised urea (absorbed blood protein) points to an upper GI source; a bleeding duodenal ulcer is the commonest.

Environmental factors have been the cause in >80% of cancers|Genetic inheritance has a role in 20% of cancers|Certain cancers can be prevented|Screening aims at detecting disease in an asymptomatic stage|Accurate diagnosis is the key to successful management
ABCDE
All are true: most cancers have environmental causes, inheritance contributes in a minority, some are preventable and screening detects asymptomatic disease.
Regarding principles of cancer surgery, which of the following statements are not true?

A 55-year-old asymptomatic man has guaiac-positive stool. Colonoscopy shows a 3-cm pedunculated sigmoid polyp, removed by snare polypectomy. Histology shows an adenoma with a focus of invasive carcinoma in the head, a 4-mm resection margin and no tumour in the stalk. What is the most appropriate next step?
CT scan|MRI scan|Surgical resection of the sigmoid colon|Observation with colonoscopic surveillance|Regular NSAID use
D
A malignant pedunculated polyp confined to the head (Haggitt 1–2) with a clear margin (>1–2 mm), well differentiated and no lymphovascular invasion is cured by polypectomy: surveillance.
After resection of colorectal liver metastases, 5-year survival is about 25–35% (up to ~40% in modern series).
A tumour 2 cm from the anal margin involves the sphincter complex, so abdominoperineal resection with permanent colostomy is needed (after neoadjuvant therapy as indicated).
Multiple colorectal adenomas in a young woman suggest FAP; Gardner syndrome is its variant with osteomas and soft-tissue tumours. Peutz–Jeghers and juvenile polyps are hamartomas.
A colonic carcinoma on colonoscopy is staged with CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis to look for liver and lung metastases before planning resection.
Adenocarcinoma, arising in Barrett mucosa, is now the commonest oesophageal cancer in the West and typically lies in the distal oesophagus.
Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with blood group A, H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, smoking and nitrosamine-rich diets.
A 60-year-old woman has recurrent squamous cell carcinoma of the anus after chemoradiation. Which operation is most appropriate?
A 68-year-old woman with faecal incontinence has a large fixed adenocarcinoma 3 cm from the anal verge. Which operation is most appropriate?
Peritoneal metastases are missed by CT and PET; staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings is the best test before gastrectomy.
Colon cancer resection needs about 5 cm of clear bowel on each side, with en bloc removal of the mesentery and lymph nodes (complete mesocolic excision).
A 68-year-old man had a colorectal adenocarcinoma resected; histology shows spread through the muscle layer into the pericolic fat but no lymph-node involvement. What Dukes stage is this?
Tumour through the muscularis propria without nodal spread is Dukes B (T3N0).
A
Cancer confined to the bowel wall (not through the muscularis propria) with no nodes or metastases is Dukes A.
